flawed_step: 0018 | Hence according to the Master theorem $T(m)=\Theta(m^0)=\Theta(1)$.
counterexample: Take all logarithms base 2 and set T(n)=0 for 1<n<=2. Let n_k=2^{2^k}. Then sqrt(n_k)=n_{k-1} and log log(n_k)=k, so T(n_k)=T(n_{k-1})+10k. Thus T(n_k)=10(1+...+k)=5k(k+1). Explicitly, T(2)=0, T(4)=10, T(16)=30, T(256)=60, and T(65536)=100. These values are unbounded, contradicting Theta(1).
assessment_summary: The substitution through step 0009 is valid (with base-2 logarithms). The Master-theorem application is not: its first case would require 10 log m=O(m^{-epsilon}) for some epsilon>0. Step 0016 instead establishes log m=o(m^{0.5}), which is a different condition. In fact S(m)=Theta((log m)^2), so T(n)=Theta((log log n)^2).
